mappings.note: Students extend a state-by-state table of crops and dishes, then explain why the food differs. LO-17 for collecting and recording survey data, LO-18 because the answer traces the diversity to soil, rainfall and climate -- a cause.
Analyse the data you collected and list the food items common across states. Interpreting one's own survey record, LO-17; no cause is asked for, so not LO-18.
Sorts foods into those eaten across many states and those peculiar to one. A classification of collected items on an observable property, LO-16.
Interview elderly people with questions you prepared, about how cooking tools changed. C-SCI2.1 names surveys explicitly, so LO-17 rather than any content outcome.
Match symptoms to a deficiency using the vitamin and mineral chart, then advise. 'Deficiency diseases with diet' is LO-18's own worked example.
Which items count as junk food, decided by comparing roasted chana with potato wafers. LO-15 for the property comparison and LO-23 for the food choice that follows, which is the LO's stated example.
Runs the copper sulphate protein test and records which foods turn violet. Investigating what nutrients a food contains is LO-17's own example.
Adds iodine, watches for blue-black and records the result in a table. A conducted investigation with recorded observations, LO-17.
The translucent-patch fat test, including drying the paper first to rule out water. Conducting an investigation and interpreting it, LO-17.
Odd one out: chana among millets, rice among pulses. Requires sorting foods into cereal and pulse groups by their dominant nutrient, LO-16.
Traditional versus modern culinary practice. Explaining processes -- slow cooking, hand grinding, fermentation -- so LO-19; LO-15 is about materials and organisms, not practices.
Ravi must frame two questions for his teacher about food as medicine. The deliverable is questions, which is CG-SCI2's goal text; no LO covers question-posing.
Tasty is not the same as nutritious -- argue it with examples. A judgement about what to eat, LO-23's 'selecting food items for a balanced diet'.
Madu's constipation traced to no vegetables and refined flour (LO-18, symptom to dietary cause), then the diet change he should make (LO-23).
Why food choices differ by region -- local crops, culture, taste. The item asks for the causes of a pattern, LO-18.
Carbohydrates as the primary energy source. LO-14 identifies materials by function among its observable features, which is what a nutrient's role is.
Potato among ghee, paneer and almonds as the carbohydrate source. Assigning foods to nutrient groups, LO-16.
Why carbohydrates and fats form the 'energy-giving' group. Names and justifies a food category, LO-16. Option (D) is truncated and its tail has leaked into the stem.
Proteins are for growth and repair of tissues. Identification by function, LO-14.
Eggs as the animal protein source among plant ones. Sorting protein sources into animal and plant classes, LO-16.
How carbohydrate and protein functions DIFFER. An explicit differentiation on the basis of function, LO-15. Option (D) is truncated with its tail in the stem.
Iodine turned the saree blue-black but not the socks -- give the reason. The item demands the cause (starch in the stiffened saree), LO-18, not merely running the test.
Why millets are healthy and whether millets alone suffice. The answer turns on needing all nutrients in proportion, which is LO-23's balanced-diet example.
Design a check for whether an unknown solution is iodine. Planning an investigation with a known starch control, LO-17.
The Taittiriya Upanishad saying that food gives life. A cultural epigraph with no scientific content an LO could hold; cited at CG-SCI3, the goal this whole chapter serves.
Locally grown crops as the main reason for regional food diversity. A cause asked for directly, LO-18.
Reshma's poor night vision: name the deficiency disease and the missing component (LO-18, deficiency disease with diet), then list four foods to add (LO-23).
Choose between canned juice, fresh juice and fresh fruit, and justify it. A day-to-day food selection, LO-23.
Why calcium and then Vitamin D for a fracture (LO-18, relating the prescription to how the body uses the nutrient), plus part (iii) which asks what question arises in the student's mind (CG-SCI2).
Sugar is a carbohydrate yet gives no blue-black -- explain. The item wants the cause: iodine detects starch, not simple sugars. LO-18 rather than LO-17, since no test is run.
Judge the claim that all starches are carbohydrates but not conversely, then DESIGN an activity to test it. LO-17 for designing the test, LO-16 for the group-and-subgroup relation being tested.
Which nutrient a growing child most needs. A dietary decision for a real person, LO-23; the bare function would be LO-14, but the item is framed as a diet choice.
Scurvy defined by its symptoms and its Vitamin C cause. Deficiency disease tied to diet, LO-18.
The citrus fruits James Lind found cured scurvy. The diet-to-disease link, LO-18; the item asks which fruits, not how Lind tested, so not LO-17.
Iodised salt introduced against goitre where soil and water lack iodine. A deficiency disorder traced to diet, LO-18.
What nutrients are, defined by what they do for the body. Identification by function, LO-14.
Water is not counted among the major nutrients. Tests the boundary of the nutrient categories, LO-16.
Vitamin D is made by the body on exposure to sunlight. Explaining a bodily process, LO-19; nothing is being identified or classified.
Why to eat some vegetables and fruit raw: heat destroys Vitamin C (LO-19, explaining the process) and so the diet should include raw items (LO-23).
Dietary fibre is also called roughage. Naming a food component by the role it plays, LO-14.
Which food group supplies roughage. Assigning foods to a component-based group, LO-16.
Constipation answered by more dietary fibre. A symptom related to its dietary cause, LO-18; the doctor's advice makes the causal link the thing marked.
How water helps the body absorb nutrients. Explaining a digestive process, LO-19.

Coluthur Gopalan, who analysed Indian foods and shaped the Mid Day Meal scheme. A biography item; cited at CG-SCI3 because his work is the application of nutrition science to everyday life, and no LO covers scientists.
The blue-black colour change that signals starch. The result of a conducted test, LO-17.
Reads a translucent oily patch from groundnut as fat. Interpreting the outcome of the paper test, LO-17.
Names copper sulphate and caustic soda as the protein reagents from Activity 3.7. Procedural knowledge of the investigation, LO-17.
Defines a balanced diet as all nutrients, roughage and water in the right amounts. LO-23 names the balanced diet as its own example.
Why frequent junk food is unhealthy -- high calories, low nutrients. An argument about what to eat, LO-23.
FSSAI as the food-quality regulator. Institutional recall with no scientific process behind it; cited at CG-SCI3, since knowing the regulator is how the learning reaches everyday food choices.
Millets called nutri-cereals for their nutrient content. Naming a food category on its properties, LO-16.
Food miles as the distance from producer to consumer, and why reducing them helps. Environmental protection, LO-24; the LO's own example set includes minimising waste of resources.
Assertion-reason on fruits, vegetables and whole grains being healthy because of their vitamins, minerals and fibre. The claim is about what makes a good diet, LO-23.

Which statements about nutrient roles are correct -- energy, body-building, small quantities. Identification by function, LO-14. The stem preserves only one of the three numbered statements its options reference.
Tiredness, bleeding gums and slow healing on a diet without fresh fruit point to Vitamin C. Deficiency disease diagnosed from diet, LO-18.
The sil-batta as the older manual grinder. A cultural-technology recall with no LO to hold it; CG-SCI3 covers the everyday-life register the question sits in.
PM POSHAN exists to give children balanced meals. A programme built on the balanced-diet principle, LO-23.
Fortification as adding micronutrients during processing. Explaining a process, LO-19; the item defines the process rather than asking what to eat.
Compares roasted chana with potato wafers on protein, fibre and fat. A property-based differentiation of two materials, LO-15.
Which is NOT a function of water -- it supplies no energy. Tests the functional identification of a food component, LO-14.
